personality_voice.book_baseline: Filch in the books is defined by a cluster of consistent traits: sadistic delight in student suffering, paranoid surveillance, explosive rage at rule-breaking, petty officiousness, and a wheezing, flat-footed physical presence that makes him simultaneously menacing and comic. His speech is characterised by hissing menace ('Sniff around, my sweet'), sudden outbursts of fury ('PEEVES!'), self-pitying complaints about the workload students create for him ('It's only a bit of mud to you, boy, but to me it's an extra hour scrubbing!'), and gleeful anticipation of punishment ('hard work and pain are the best teachers if you ask me'). He has a streak of genuine cruelty: he fantasises explicitly about hanging students by their wrists and whipping them, and he leers over students being sent into the Forbidden Forest at night. He is also marked by a deep social insecurity — he is a Squib in a magical world, bitter and humiliated, which Ron explicitly identifies as the source of his hatred of students. His emotional range extends to genuine distress (his grief over Mrs Norris), genuine joy (securing the approval-for-whipping form under Umbridge), and genuine fear (his helpless rage at Peeves). His voice is nasal, wheezing, and oscillates between sycophantic obsequiousness toward authority figures and vicious contempt for students.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The films preserve Filch's visual identity (wheezing, flat-footed, accompanied by Mrs Norris), his surveillance function, his delight in student punishment, and his antagonistic presence. Key book lines survive almost verbatim: 'A pity they let the old punishments die. There was a time detention would find you hanging by your thumbs in the dungeons. God, I miss the screaming' (CoS film). His leer as he escorts students to the forest, his gleeful malice at the Yule Ball (comically 'dancing' with Mrs Norris), and his eager participation in Umbridge's regime are all present. His voice and physical manner — David Bradley's performance — faithfully captures the wheezing, hunched, paranoid caretaker.
personality_voice.difference: The films largely preserve Filch's dominant personality traits. The main losses are: (1) his internal voice and monologue — the books allow us to witness his muttered obsessions ('great sizzling dragon bogies… make an example… where's the form') which build texture; (2) his extended speech patterns across long scenes like the Hogsmeade Secrecy Sensor incidents in GoF and OotP, where he shows paranoid self-importance and elaborate suspicion, are reduced to brief functional appearances; (3) his pathetic, self-pitying register ('It's only a bit of mud to you, boy, but to me it's an extra hour scrubbing!') disappears entirely — his vulnerability is stripped away. The Kwikspell/Squib scene, which in the books shows Filch's desperate shame and emotional fragility, is cut from the theatrical release (per the non-theatrical exclusion note). This is a meaningful loss of secondary trait texture, though his dominant sadistic and paranoid traits survive.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: Dominant personality traits (sadism, surveillance obsession, delight in punishment, obsequiousness toward authority) are preserved and performed effectively. The penalty is for loss of secondary emotional texture: his self-pity, his internal muttering register, his pathetic vulnerability around the Squib identity, and the full range of his paranoid speech patterns across multiple books. These are real reductions but do not destroy the recognisability of the character. Score: 19.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: Filch serves multiple narrative functions across the books: (1) as an active obstacle to the protagonists — he pursues them, catches them, threatens them, and forces them into plot-altering decisions; (2) as an informant and enforcer for authority (Umbridge in OotP, Snape throughout); (3) as a comic antagonist whose defeats by Peeves or the twins provide recurring structural relief; (4) as a plot driver: his Kwikspell letter in CoS triggers an important revelation (Squib identity), and his confiscation of the Marauder's Map establishes backstory. He also functions as a barometer for the school's moral atmosphere — his enthusiasm under Umbridge signals the regime's darkness. He is active: he patrols, pursues, reports, threatens, and catches students. He initiates confrontations regularly.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: The films preserve Filch's role as obstacle (CoS corridor chase, detention escort), enforcer (OotP Umbridge alliance, GoF Secrecy Sensor checks), and comic antagonist (Yule Ball dancing, PoA searching portraits). He retains agency in discrete scenes: he escorts students to detention, checks names against lists, patrols corridors, and reports to Umbridge. In DH2 he bursts in shouting about students out of bed. His role as informant/enforcer is intact.
narrative_role_agency.difference: Two significant agency losses: (1) The Kwikspell/Squib confrontation scene is cut from the theatrical release. In the books this is a scene where Filch exercises real narrative agency — he nearly punishes Harry, is distracted by Peeves, then discovers Harry may have read his letter, and his emotional reaction drives the scene. In the film this becomes a brief comic beat (the envelope dropped and snatched back) that strips the Squib revelation of its dramatic weight and removes Filch's agency over the moment entirely. (2) His extended Umbridge alliance in OotP — where he patrols for secret passages, is tipped off about Dungbombs, acts as Umbridge's instrument against the DA — is significantly compressed. Several of his active investigative moves (boarding up passages, prowling for DA members) are reduced to background decoration. His pursuit scenes in the Marauder's Map/staircase sequences in GoF are present but brief.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: Filch's structural role as obstacle and enforcer is preserved, and he retains enough active agency in individual scenes to remain functionally the same character. But the Kwikspell scene's theatrical cut removes a key moment of his independent agency, and his OotP investigative role is compressed into background. His role is reduced but recognisable. Score: 14.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Filch's motivations are clearly established in the books: (1) a deep, bitter resentment of magical students born from his own Squib status — he cannot do what they do, so he hates them for it; (2) a sadistic desire for authority and punishment as compensation for his powerlessness in the magical hierarchy; (3) a genuine attachment to Mrs Norris as his only real emotional relationship; (4) a desire for institutional legitimacy — he wants official sanction to punish students severely, which is why he aligns with Umbridge so eagerly; (5) an obsession with order and cleanliness that functions as a displacement activity for his deeper frustrations. These motivations are interconnected: the Squib identity explains all of them. Ron's analysis ('He's bitter') is the books' explicit gloss.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The films establish Filch's motivations adequately: his sadism, his desire to punish, and his alignment with authority are all preserved. His attachment to Mrs Norris is shown in his distress at her Petrification in CoS. His eagerness under Umbridge is present. However, the Squib motivation is handled differently: in the film, the Kwikspell/Squib revelation is stripped of its theatrical weight (the scene is cut from theatrical release), so the explicit link between his powerlessness and his bitterness is never fully dramatised. Ron delivers the exposition ('He's bitter. He's a Squib') in the CoS film corridor scene, so the information is present — but without the emotionally charged Filch confrontation around his Kwikspell letter, the motivation feels stated rather than experienced.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: The core motivations (bitterness, desire for punishment authority, Mrs Norris attachment) survive. The loss is that the Squib identity, which in the books is a moment of acute vulnerability and humiliation that makes Filch three-dimensional, is reduced to exposition in the film. The internal conflict — his shame at his own inadequacy — is named but not dramatised. This is a meaningful simplification: the motivation exists but is underexplained.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: Motivations are present but simplified. The Squib shame-as-motivation is stated via Ron's dialogue but stripped of its experiential weight. The sadism-as-compensation dynamic is implied but never as explicitly shown as in the books. Score: 10.

character_arc.book_baseline: Filch's arc is essentially flat across the seven books — he is consistently the same bitter, sadistic caretaker from start to finish. However, there is a meaningful structural development across the series: (1) he begins as a low-level obstacle; (2) in CoS he receives his most significant characterisation (Squib revelation, Mrs Norris Petrification, office scene); (3) in OotP he reaches a dark apex under Umbridge, becoming genuinely frightening as an instrument of institutional cruelty; (4) in HBP and DH he is reduced to background patrol; (5) in DH2 he appears briefly in the Great Hall aftermath — a survivor in the wreckage. The flat arc is intentional: Filch never grows or changes, and that stasis is itself characterisation. His DH2 appearance — communing quietly with Mrs Norris amid the dead — is a quiet coda that fits the character exactly.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The films preserve the flat arc faithfully. Filch is the same character in Philosopher's Stone as in Deathly Hallows Part 2. His OotP apex under Umbridge is compressed but present. His DH2 appearance in the Great Hall aftermath is intact (he is shown communing with Mrs Norris after the battle). The flat arc is preserved.
character_arc.difference: The arc is correctly flat in both books and films. The OotP material is somewhat compressed — his enthusiastic anticipation of whipping powers, his horror-whip form procurement, and his patrolling with a horsewhip are reduced — but the essential arc trajectory is unchanged. No arc is invented or distorted.
character_arc.penalty_logic: A flat arc is appropriate for this character and the films honour it. Some compression of the OotP apex, but not enough to distort the arc. Score: 13.

key_relationships.book_baseline: Filch has three key relationships in the books: (1) Mrs Norris — his only genuine emotional bond, treated as a beloved companion and extension of himself; (2) Peeves — a decades-long antagonism that is one of the most consistent recurring dynamics in the series, with Peeves's torment of Filch providing structural comic relief and regularly driving Filch into apoplectic rage; (3) Umbridge — a relationship of enthusiastic mutual exploitation in OotP, where Filch sees her regime as his chance for revenge and she uses his knowledge of the school; (4) students generally — his adversarial relationship with the student body is his defining social orientation. The Peeves dynamic in particular is a crucial source of characterisation across many books.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: Mrs Norris's relationship is preserved — his distress at her Petrification in CoS is emotionally present, and his communing with her in DH2's aftermath is intact. The Umbridge alliance is shown in OotP, though compressed. The relationship with students is maintained through his antagonistic patrol function. However, Peeves does not appear in the films at all, which eliminates an entire relational dynamic that generates much of Filch's most vivid characterisation across the books.
key_relationships.difference: The complete absence of Peeves from the films is a significant loss. In the books, Filch vs Peeves is one of the most consistent and characteristically rich relationships — it shows Filch's impotence against genuinely chaotic forces, his obsessive rage, and his pathetic dependency on rules that Peeves simply ignores. Several of the most vivid Filch scenes in the books (the trophy room chase in SS, the staircase confrontation in GoF, the dungeon-oil-lamp scene in CoS, his apoplectic pursuit across multiple books) are structured around Peeves. The films cannot replicate this dynamic. The Mrs Norris and Umbridge relationships are adequately preserved.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: The Peeves relationship is entirely absent from the films. This is a substantial alteration of a key relational dynamic that drives many of Filch's most characterful scenes and reveals his impotence, his rage, and his pathos. The Mrs Norris and student relationships survive. Score: 7.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: Filch's complexity in the books rests on several layers: (1) the Squib identity as a source of genuine pathos — he is a man humiliated by the world he lives in, compensating through petty authority; (2) the Peeves antagonism as a window into his impotent rage; (3) the office scenes (CoS) which show his vulnerability, his shame, his disorder (frog brains, muttering about punishments), and the unexpected moment where his discovery of the Kwikspell letter reduces him to incoherent stammering; (4) his complex relationship with authority — he is simultaneously a bully to students and a servile subordinate to teachers; (5) his Christmas dinner appearance in CoS (in formal dress, slightly pitiable); (6) his enjoyment of Umbridge's regime which is darkly comic because it reveals how genuinely damaged he is. The books give him enough recurring texture that his flat-arc presence is never boring.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The films capture some of this complexity: the CoS Petrification scene preserves his distress about Mrs Norris and his desperate accusation of Harry. The OotP Umbridge scenes show his gleeful alignment with institutional cruelty. The Yule Ball dancing scene is a brief humanising/comic moment. But large portions of the book texture are lost: the CoS office scene (cut from theatrical release), the extended OotP Squib/surveillance material, the GoF staircase-and-egg scene where his interaction with Snape and Moody shows his complicated position in the school hierarchy, his muttering voice as self-revelation, and above all the entire Peeves dynamic which produces so much of his most nuanced characterisation.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: The films retain Filch as a recognisable surface but lose the layered texture that makes him more than a recurring comic obstacle. The Squib pathos is stated but not dramatised. The Peeves antagonism is absent. The office scene complexity is cut. The GoF egg/staircase scene — one of the most revealing passages for understanding Filch's position in the hierarchy — is reduced to a brief appearance. What remains is a faithful sketch of the character's dominant traits without the contradictions and vulnerabilities that give him depth.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: Noticeable simplification. The most important nuances — Squib shame as dramatised vulnerability, Peeves antagonism as structural characterisation, the office scene fragility — are missing or reduced. The character remains recognisable but is hollowed of the material that made him complex. Score: 9.

lost_or_transferred_material: Filch's CoS office scene: his muttering, his punishment-form obsession, his emotional collapse upon discovering Harry may have read the Kwikspell letter — cut from theatrical release
Filch's Squib identity as a dramatised source of pathos and vulnerability (survives only as Ron's exposition)
The entire Peeves vs Filch relationship — Peeves does not appear in the films at all, removing Filch's most consistent relational antagonism
Filch's extended OotP activity: boarding up passages, prowling with a horsewhip, his anticipation of whipping powers described in detail
Filch's GoF staircase scene with Snape and Moody — present in screenplay but highly compressed in theatrical cut, loses the complexity of his position in the school hierarchy
Filch's self-pitying, muttering internal voice across multiple book scenes (CoS punishment-form scene, the 'only a bit of mud to you' confrontation)
Filch's pathetic formality at the Christmas dinner in CoS (old tailcoat, moldy appearance)
Multiple scenes of Filch's gleeful anticipation of punishment in the Forbidden Forest detention (book version is far more extended and characterful than the film equivalent)
score_caps_applied: Cap 2 (score above 80 if key relationships change substantially): Applied — the complete absence of Peeves from the films removes one of Filch's most structurally significant relationships. This prevents a score above 80.
Cap 1 (score above 85 if films remove major complexity): Applied in alignment with above — the loss of the Peeves dynamic and the Squib-shame dramatisation removes major complexity.
comparative.key_observations: Filch's core identity — the sadistic, wheezing, paranoid caretaker who polices students with gleeful malice and pathetic authority — survives the adaptation effectively. His dominant personality traits, flat arc, and relationship with Mrs Norris are faithfully preserved, and David Bradley's performance captures the essential voice and physicality. The principal losses are threefold: the complete absence of Peeves eliminates his most recurring and structurally rich antagonistic relationship; the theatrical cut of the CoS Kwikspell/Squib office scene removes the one moment where his internal vulnerability is directly dramatised; and his self-pitying, muttering interiority — a key source of his book texture — disappears almost entirely from the films. The result is a recognisable but somewhat flattened version of the character: the surface is faithful, but the layers of pathos, shame, and impotent rage that make him more than a recurring obstacle are substantially thinned. He scores in the mid-70s because what the films show is genuinely accurate, but what they omit meaningfully reduces the completeness of the portrayal.
